lead: SONET in North America and SDH elsewhere define one synchronous frame that carries many low-rate channels on a single optical line. One master clock and byte interleaving let any channel be added or dropped without taking the whole signal apart. The frame repeats every 125 µs, so every rate is an exact multiple of 51.84 Mb/s. Telephone companies built voice, leased-line and protected-ring networks on it, and packet networks still use it as a reliable pipe.
prereq: You need: time-division multiplexing of digital voice channels into the E1 (2.048 Mb/s) and T1 (1.544 Mb/s) carriers, and the ring and protection terms of Optical network concepts.

blocks.text: The older plesiochronous digital hierarchy (PDH) let every multiplexer run on its own, nearly equal clock and used bit stuffing to make up the difference. To pick one 2 Mb/s line out of a 140 Mb/s stream, the operator had to demultiplex step by step down to that line and build everything up again. SONET (North America) and SDH (Europe, India and most of the world) replace this with one synchronous frame: every node locks to a primary reference clock, and bytes from many channels sit in fixed, known positions.

The SONET building block is the STS-1 electrical signal at 51.84 Mb/s; its optical form is OC-1. STS-n and OC-n run at n × 51.84 Mb/s. The SDH building block is STM-1 at 155.52 Mb/s, which equals STS-3/OC-3, and STM-N runs at N × 155.52 Mb/s.

A pointer in the line overhead marks where the synchronous payload envelope (SPE) starts inside the frame. If a tributary clock runs slightly fast or slow, the pointer moves by one byte and a stuffing byte is added or removed, so the payload floats in the frame without a slip. Concatenation, written STS-3c, ties three STS-1 payloads into one container with one pointer; the SDH VC-4 does the same job.

The STS-1 frame is a rectangle of 90 columns × 9 rows = 810 bytes, sent row by row. It lasts 125 µs, so 8000 frames pass per second. The first 3 columns are transport overhead: section overhead in rows 1 to 3 and line overhead in rows 4 to 9, with the pointer bytes H1, H2 and H3 in row 4. The other 87 columns form the SPE, 87 × 9 = 783 bytes, whose first column is the path overhead.

blocks.where: R is the bit rate in b/s; 8 bits per byte; 8000 frames per second. For STS-1, R = 810 × 8 × 8000 = 51.84 Mb/s; each column of 9 bytes is worth 9 × 8 × 8000 = 576 kb/s.

blocks.text: So the SPE carries 783 × 64 000 = 50.112 Mb/s. Take away the path overhead column and two fixed-stuff columns and 84 columns of user payload remain: 48.384 Mb/s, room for 28 T1s or one DS3 (44.736 Mb/s).

The STM-1 frame is 270 columns × 9 rows = 2430 bytes in the same 125 µs. Its first 9 columns are the section overhead: the regenerator section overhead in rows 1 to 3, the AU pointer in row 4 and the multiplex section overhead in rows 5 to 9. The other 261 columns carry the VC-4, whose first column is path overhead and whose remaining 260 columns are the C-4 container, 149.76 Mb/s. E1s enter the VC-4 through TU-12s grouped 3 into a TUG-2, 7 TUG-2s into a TUG-3 and 3 TUG-3s into the VC-4: 3 × 7 × 3 = 63 E1s.

SONET has four layers. The photonic layer is the light on the fiber. The section layer (SDH: regenerator section) runs between regenerators and handles framing and section error checks. The line layer (SDH: multiplex section) runs between multiplexers and carries the pointer, protection switching signals and line error checks. The path layer runs end to end between the nodes that build and read the payload. Each layer checks its own overhead, so a fault can be located to one section of the route.

An add-drop multiplexer (ADM) uses the fixed byte positions: it drops selected tributaries, inserts new traffic into the same positions and passes the rest, with no full demultiplexing. In a UPSR (unidirectional path-switched ring), called SNCP in SDH, each signal is sent both ways round the ring and the receiver selects the better copy. In a two-fiber BLSR (bidirectional line-switched ring), called MS-SPRing in SDH, half the capacity of each fiber is kept as shared protection, and at a cut the nodes beside it loop the working traffic back onto that protection capacity. Both restore traffic within 50 ms.
Jitter is short-term variation of the clock phase, at 10 Hz and above; wander is slow drift below 10 Hz. Pointers absorb wander, and interface specifications limit jitter.

examples.question: An STS-1 frame is 810 bytes and repeats 8000 times per second. (a) Find the line rate. (b) Find the SPE rate for the 783-byte envelope. (c) What fraction of the frame is transport overhead? (d) What fraction is overhead of any kind if the path overhead column is also counted?
steps: (b) SPE bits per frame = 783 × 8 = 6264. SPE rate = 6264 × 8000 = 50.112 Mb/s.
(c) Transport overhead = 810 − 783 = 27 bytes (3 columns × 9 rows). Fraction = 27/810 = 0.0333 = 3.33 percent, worth 1.728 Mb/s.
(d) Adding the path overhead column: 27 + 9 = 36 bytes. Fraction = 36/810 = 4.44 percent, and 51.84 × (1 − 0.0444) = 49.536 Mb/s is left before the fixed stuff is removed.
examples.answer: Line rate 51.84 Mb/s, SPE rate 50.112 Mb/s, transport overhead 3.33 percent, all overhead 4.44 percent.

examples.question: An STM-1 frame has 270 columns × 9 rows and repeats every 125 µs. (a) Find the STM-1 rate and show it equals three STS-1s. (b) Find the STM-16 rate. (c) Find the VC-4 and C-4 rates. (d) How many E1s does one STM-1 carry, and what is their total rate?
steps: (d) The mapping 3 × 7 × 3 gives 63 E1s. Their rate is 63 × 2.048 = 129.024 Mb/s.

Check: 155.52 ÷ 2.048 = 75.9, but only 63 E1s fit, because each E1 sits in a TU-12 of 36 bytes per frame (2.304 Mb/s) with its own overhead and stuffing, and the section overhead takes 9 of the 270 columns.

traps: The 810-byte frame belongs to STS-1. An STM-1 (or STS-3) frame is 2430 bytes, 270 × 9, in the same 125 µs.
Do not divide 155.52 Mb/s by 2.048 Mb/s to count E1s; that gives 75.9. The SDH mapping is 3 × 7 × 3 = 63 E1s per STM-1.
Pointer bytes H1, H2 and H3 sit in row 4 of the transport overhead, not inside the SPE. They mark where the floating envelope starts.
The 783-byte SPE still contains the path overhead; transport overhead alone is 3.33 percent, all overhead 4.44 percent.
UPSR/SNCP sends the signal both ways and selects; BLSR/MS-SPRing shares protection capacity and loops back at the cut. Do not swap the two.

quiz.q: State the STS-1 and STM-1 rates and the SONET signal equal to STM-1.
What does the section layer monitor?
quiz.a: Framing and section error bytes between regenerators (the regenerator section in SDH).

quiz.q: Why does a synchronous frame use pointers?
quiz.a: Pointers let the SPE float inside the frame, so a small clock difference is absorbed by a one-byte pointer move and stuffing, without demultiplexing the payload or slipping data.

quiz.q: An STS-1 frame has 3 columns of transport overhead and 1 column of path overhead out of 90. Find the SPE bytes and the SPE rate.
quiz.a: SPE columns = 90 − 3 = 87; SPE bytes = 87 × 9 = 783; SPE rate = 783 × 8 × 8000 = 50.112 Mb/s.

quiz.q: How many STM-1s fit in one STM-64, and what is the STM-64 rate?
quiz.a: 64 STM-1s. STM-64 = 64 × 155.52 = 9953.28 Mb/s, about 10 Gb/s, which is OC-192.

quiz.q: An STM-1 carries 63 E1s. Explain why their total rate is well below 155.52 Mb/s.
quiz.a: 63 × 2.048 = 129.024 Mb/s. The difference is overhead at every level: 9 columns of section overhead and pointer (5.184 Mb/s), the VC-4 path overhead column (0.576 Mb/s), and inside the C-4 the TU-12 and VC-12 overhead and stuffing of each E1, which uses 2.304 Mb/s of TU-12 capacity for 2.048 Mb/s of data.

quiz.q: A ring must survive one fiber cut within 50 ms. Compare UPSR and BLSR.
quiz.a: UPSR sends every path both ways round the ring and the receiver selects, so no signalling is needed at a cut, but each path uses capacity on the whole ring. BLSR keeps half of each fiber as shared protection and loops working traffic back at the nodes beside the cut, so capacity can be reused around the ring. Both are specified for restoration within 50 ms.

beyond: Not for the exam. SONET/SDH is still present in metro, utility and railway networks because it gives fixed delay and fast protection. New high-rate systems use the optical transport network (OTN, ITU-T G.709), which wraps SONET/SDH and Ethernet into larger containers. Synchronous Ethernet and IEEE 1588 PTP now carry timing for packet networks. Search OTN, GFP, SyncE and PTP.
